key_insight: Surface small polarons on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) are far less mobile than in bulk because surface geometry removes many favorable hopping pathways.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous rutile TiO2 can show much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, which matters for catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy-storage device performance.
method: Machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics extended from bulk oxides to reduced oxide surfaces
Long-timescale simulations spanning several nanoseconds across multiple temperatures
Applied to oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) to resolve hopping pathways and vacancy effects
evidence_signal: The study uses nanosecond-scale finite-temperature dynamics and finds several-orders-of-magnitude lower surface polaron mobility than in the corresponding bulk material.
watch_item: The conclusions are demonstrated for a paradigmatic rutile TiO2(110) surface, so transferability to other oxide surfaces should be validated case by case.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
